title: Tracheostomy: Airway Patency First
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
bottomLine: A tracheostomy is an airway. New respiratory distress, inability to pass suction catheter, absent airflow, sudden desaturation, or accidental decannulation requires immediate airway-focused action and escalation according to the patient's maturity of stoma and emergency plan.
recognize: Thick secretions, visible mucus, coarse breath sounds, increased work of breathing, and falling oxygenation can indicate obstruction.
Fresh tracheostomies are higher risk for false-passage creation during reinsertion.
priorities: Assess breathing, airflow through the tube, oxygenation, and tube position.
Suction when clinically indicated using the prescribed technique, not on a fixed schedule alone.
Keep emergency equipment available, including appropriate replacement tracheostomy tubes and obturator per policy.
assessMonitor: Trend respiratory effort, breath sounds, secretions, stoma/skin, cuff pressure when applicable, and humidification.
interventions: Provide humidification and hydration as appropriate to prevent thick secretions.
Use sterile/clean suction technique according to setting and policy while minimizing suction duration and trauma.
medicationSafety: Preoxygenation may be needed for selected patients before suctioning; avoid unnecessary saline instillation unless specifically indicated by protocol.
teaching: Teach caregivers the individualized emergency plan and signs of obstruction or dislodgement.
delegationScope: Tracheostomy care/suctioning delegation depends on state, setting, and competency; airway deterioration requires immediate licensed clinical response.
examTrap: Leaving the bedside without emergency tracheostomy equipment available.
oneLinePearl: A trach problem is an airway problem until proven otherwise.

title: Chest Tubes: Keep the System Working
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
bottomLine: Chest-drainage care is about restoring pleural pressure safely. Keep the system below chest level and connections secure; sudden dyspnea, new absent breath sounds, rapidly increasing subcutaneous emphysema, large fresh blood loss, or accidental tube dislodgement requires immediate escalation.
recognize: Tidaling can vary with breathing and may stop when the lung re-expands or when tubing is obstructed.
Continuous bubbling in a water-seal chamber may indicate an air leak depending on the system.
priorities: Assess patient respiratory status before troubleshooting the device.
Keep drainage unit upright and below chest level.
Do not routinely clamp a chest tube unless specifically ordered or required briefly by an established protocol.
assessMonitor: Trend breath sounds, oxygenation, work of breathing, drainage amount/color, insertion site, tubing patency, and subcutaneous emphysema.
interventions: If the tube disconnects from the drainage system, follow facility protocol to re-establish a sterile closed system promptly.
If the tube comes out of the patient, cover the site per emergency protocol and call for immediate help.
medicationSafety: Coordinate analgesia because pain limits deep breathing and mobility.
teaching: Avoid pulling on tubing and call for help before mobilizing if unsure how to manage the drainage system.
delegationScope: Routine mobility assistance may be delegated after a plan is established; chest-tube assessment and troubleshooting remain licensed-nurse responsibilities.
examTrap: Clamping a bubbling chest tube as the first response to an air leak.
oneLinePearl: Assess the patient first, then the chest-drainage system.

title: Central Lines: Prevent CLABSI
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological Therapies
bottomLine: Central-line infection prevention depends on meticulous hand hygiene, hub disinfection, aseptic access, intact dressings, and removing lines that are no longer needed. Fever, rigors, hypotension, or line-site inflammation during infusion can signal bloodstream infection and requires rapid evaluation.
recognize: A normal-looking insertion site does not rule out catheter-related bloodstream infection.
Every unnecessary line-day creates avoidable infection risk.
priorities: Disinfect access ports for the required duration and allow appropriate drying.
Maintain clean, dry, intact dressings and use aseptic technique for access.
Report systemic infection signs promptly and obtain ordered cultures correctly.
assessMonitor: Assess site, dressing integrity, necessity, fever/chills, hemodynamics, and infusion complications.
interventions: Do not access a central line through visibly contaminated equipment.
Replace dressings/caps according to evidence-based facility policy and contamination events.
medicationSafety: Use lumen compatibility guidance to avoid precipitates or incompatible infusions.
redFlags: New severe dyspnea after line manipulation
teaching: Keep the dressing dry and report fever, drainage, pain, swelling, or a loose dressing.
delegationScope: Central-line access and dressing-change scope varies for LPN/LVN practice; infection assessment requires licensed-nurse escalation.
examTrap: Keeping an unused central line 'just in case.'
oneLinePearl: Scrub the hub, protect the dressing, remove the line when unnecessary.
sourceBasis: CDC Guidelines for Prevention of Intravascular Catheter-Related Infections

title: Central-Line Air Embolism
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Sudden dyspnea, chest pain, cough, confusion, hypoxemia, or cardiovascular collapse after central-line disconnection/removal can indicate venous air embolism. Clamp/occlude the source immediately if possible, call emergency help, give high-concentration oxygen, and position/manage according to the emergency protocol.
recognize: Risk is highest when an open venous catheter is above or exposed to negative intrathoracic pressure.
Line disconnection or improper removal technique can allow air entry.
priorities: Prevent further air entry by clamping or occluding the catheter/source.
Activate emergency response and give oxygen.
Position according to institutional protocol while avoiding delays in definitive resuscitation.
assessMonitor: Monitor airway, breathing, circulation, oxygenation, neurologic status, and rhythm.
interventions: Use occlusive dressings and proper removal technique to prevent air entry.
Ensure all line connections are secure.
teaching: Patients should avoid manipulating central-line connections and report loose or disconnected tubing immediately.
delegationScope: Suspected air embolism is an emergency and cannot be delegated.
examTrap: Leaving an open central-line hub uncapped while gathering supplies.
oneLinePearl: Open central line + sudden dyspnea = stop air entry and resuscitate.
sourceBasis: AHRQ central venous catheter safety resources

title: Urinary Catheters: Prevent CAUTI
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: The strongest CAUTI-prevention strategy is avoiding unnecessary catheterization and removing the catheter as soon as the indication ends. Maintain a closed system, unobstructed flow, dependent drainage, and routine hygiene rather than antimicrobial irrigation.
recognize: Cloudy or foul-smelling urine alone does not establish symptomatic UTI.
Older adults with catheters frequently have bacteriuria without infection.
priorities: Verify ongoing indication daily.
Keep the drainage bag below bladder level and off the floor.
Maintain closed connections and unobstructed tubing.
assessMonitor: Assess urine output, suprapubic/flank pain, fever, catheter obstruction, hematuria, and systemic illness rather than appearance alone.
interventions: Perform routine perineal hygiene and secure the catheter to reduce urethral trauma.
Obtain urine specimens from the sampling port using aseptic technique rather than from the drainage bag.
medicationSafety: Do not use prophylactic antibiotics solely because an indwelling catheter is present unless specifically indicated.
redFlags: No urine with bladder distention/obstruction concern
teaching: Do not disconnect the system unnecessarily and keep the bag below bladder level.
delegationScope: Catheter care and output measurement may be delegated if policy permits; new infection/obstruction signs require licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Sending a urine culture because the urine looks cloudy in an otherwise asymptomatic chronically catheterized patient.
oneLinePearl: Best CAUTI prevention: no catheter unless needed, out as soon as possible.
sourceBasis: CDC Guideline for Prevention of Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infections

title: Enteral Feeding: Aspiration and Tube Safety
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Enteral nutrition is preferred when the GI tract works, but aspiration and tube misplacement can be dangerous. Verify tube placement according to the device/facility protocol before initial use and as required thereafter, elevate the head of bed when appropriate, and stop feeding for acute respiratory distress or suspected displacement.
recognize: Coughing, choking, vomiting, abdominal distention, new respiratory symptoms, or unexpected tube length can signal a problem.
Auscultating air over the stomach is not a reliable method to confirm tube placement.
priorities: Verify initial placement by the accepted method before feeding/medication use.
Maintain head-of-bed elevation during feeding when not contraindicated.
Flush the tube as ordered to maintain patency and separate incompatible medications.
assessMonitor: Trend tolerance, abdominal findings, stool, hydration, weight, respiratory status, glucose/electrolytes as relevant, and tube position markers.
interventions: Use feeding pumps and rates as ordered.
Do not mix all medications together with formula; give each medication appropriately and flush between agents as needed.
medicationSafety: Do not crush enteric-coated, extended-release, sublingual, or other unsuitable formulations for tube administration.
Check medication-feed interactions when absorption is important.
teaching: Caregivers need device-specific instructions for position checks, flushing, feeding setup, and signs of aspiration.
delegationScope: Enteral feeding/medication scope varies by setting and state; aspiration assessment remains a licensed-nurse responsibility.
examTrap: Confirming nasogastric placement by injecting air and listening over the stomach.
oneLinePearl: Tube feeding is safe only when placement, position, and aspiration risk are controlled.
sourceBasis: ASPEN safe-practice recommendations for enteral nutrition

title: Parenteral Nutrition: Glucose, Line, Electrolytes
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Parenteral nutrition is high-risk therapy requiring dedicated line practices, glucose monitoring, electrolyte/volume surveillance, and infection prevention. Abrupt interruption of a high-dextrose infusion can cause hypoglycemia in some patients, so follow the ordered contingency plan when infusion unexpectedly stops.
recognize: Hyperglycemia, electrolyte shifts, fluid overload, liver abnormalities, and catheter infection are major risks.
Severely malnourished patients are at risk for refeeding syndrome after nutrition starts.
priorities: Verify solution, rate, route, line, and pump settings.
Monitor glucose and ordered electrolytes closely, especially during initiation/changes.
Maintain strict central-line asepsis.
assessMonitor: Trend glucose, potassium, magnesium, phosphate, sodium, weight, fluid balance, liver tests, triglycerides when ordered, and line infection signs.
interventions: Use a dedicated lumen when required by policy.
Never speed up PN to catch up after an interruption.
medicationSafety: Compatibility with PN is complex; do not piggyback medications without verified compatibility.
Use the prescribed dextrose fallback if PN is unexpectedly unavailable and hypoglycemia risk exists.
teaching: Home PN patients need strict line-care education and immediate reporting of fever or catheter problems.
delegationScope: PN administration and central-line scope vary for LPN/LVN practice; metabolic deterioration requires licensed-nurse/provider management.
examTrap: Increasing the infusion rate to make up missed PN volume.
oneLinePearl: PN is a medication: verify it, protect the line, and watch glucose/electrolytes.

title: Refeeding Syndrome
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
bottomLine: After prolonged undernutrition, rapidly increasing calories—especially carbohydrate—can drive phosphate, potassium, and magnesium into cells and cause dangerous fluid/electrolyte shifts. High-risk patients need cautious nutrition initiation and close electrolyte monitoring.
recognize: Risk rises with very low intake, major weight loss, eating disorders, alcohol use disorder, malabsorption, prolonged fasting, or severe chronic illness.
Weakness, edema, dyspnea, confusion, seizures, or arrhythmias after feeding begins can be clues.
priorities: Identify high-risk patients before aggressive feeding.
Check and replace phosphate, potassium, magnesium, and thiamine as ordered.
Escalate new cardiorespiratory or neurologic symptoms promptly.
assessMonitor: Trend electrolytes, glucose, fluid balance, weight, edema, respiratory status, rhythm, and neurologic status during early refeeding.
interventions: Advance calories according to the nutrition plan rather than rapidly reaching full targets.
Avoid unnecessary sodium/fluid overload.
medicationSafety: Thiamine supplementation is commonly used in high-risk patients before/during refeeding according to protocol.
teaching: Explain why nutrition may need to increase gradually despite understandable urgency to restore weight.
delegationScope: Intake/weight collection may be delegated, but electrolyte/clinical interpretation requires licensed-nurse/provider management.
examTrap: Starting full-calorie feeding immediately in a severely malnourished patient without electrolyte planning.
oneLinePearl: Starved cells + sudden carbs = phosphate crash risk.
sourceBasis: ASPEN Consensus Recommendations for Refeeding Syndrome

title: Dysphagia and Aspiration Prevention
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Coughing with meals, wet/gurgly voice, food pocketing, recurrent pneumonia, drooling, or prolonged chewing can signal dysphagia. Stop oral intake when swallowing safety is uncertain, position upright, and obtain swallowing evaluation rather than simply thickening everything without assessment.
recognize: Stroke, Parkinson disease, dementia, neuromuscular disease, head/neck cancer, and reduced alertness increase risk.
Silent aspiration can occur without coughing.
priorities: Assess alertness and ability to manage secretions before feeding.
Use the prescribed texture/liquid consistency and swallowing strategies.
Keep upright during meals and for the instructed period afterward.
assessMonitor: Monitor cough, voice quality, respiratory status, meal duration, intake, weight, hydration, and recurrent fevers/pneumonia.
interventions: Provide small bites/sips and pacing according to speech-language pathology recommendations.
Perform oral care because oral bacterial burden contributes to aspiration pneumonia risk.
medicationSafety: Verify whether pills can be crushed or require alternate formulations; do not crush extended-release or enteric-coated products indiscriminately.
teaching: Caregivers should use the exact swallowing plan rather than improvising food consistency.
delegationScope: Feeding assistance may be delegated only after a safe plan is established for a stable patient; new coughing/choking requires immediate stop and licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Continuing to feed a coughing post-stroke patient because oxygen saturation is still normal.
oneLinePearl: If swallowing safety is uncertain, stop feeding and assess before the next bite.

title: Oxygen Therapy and Fire Safety
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: Oxygen supports combustion. Use the prescribed device/flow, keep oxygen away from smoking/open flames/sparks and oil-based products, secure cylinders, and reassess the patient—not just the pulse oximeter—when oxygen needs rise.
recognize: Worsening oxygen requirement can signal clinical deterioration such as pneumonia, pulmonary edema, PE, pneumothorax, or hypoventilation.
Pulse oximetry can be inaccurate with poor perfusion, motion, some dyshemoglobinemias, and device factors.
priorities: Verify oxygen source, device, flow, fit, and humidification when indicated.
Post/enforce no-smoking/fire precautions.
Escalate unexplained increasing oxygen need or respiratory distress.
assessMonitor: Trend respiratory rate/effort, mental status, oxygenation, skin/mucosa, device pressure areas, and underlying disease.
interventions: Use water-based lubricants around oxygen equipment rather than petroleum products.
Store cylinders secured upright or in approved racks.
medicationSafety: Oxygen is a medication in clinical settings and should be titrated to ordered targets/protocol; excessive oxygen can be harmful in selected conditions.
teaching: No smoking or open flames near home oxygen; keep equipment away from heat sources and follow supplier safety instructions.
delegationScope: Routine device checks may be shared, but oxygen titration authority and assessment of deterioration depend on scope/order/protocol.
examTrap: Turning up oxygen repeatedly without assessing why the patient is worsening.
oneLinePearl: Oxygen is treatment—and a fire accelerant.
